name: Avobenzone
lead: Avobenzone (butyl methoxydibenzoylmethane, trade name Parsol 1789) is an oil-soluble organic compound used as a UVA filter in chemical sunscreens and in moisturisers and cosmetics that carry an SPF claim [1][2]. It absorbs ultraviolet light across much of the UVA range, with an absorption peak near 357 nm [2].

It is notable for being the main UVA-absorbing organic filter permitted in the United States, at up to 3%, while the European Union permits up to 5% [2]. It is photounstable, losing absorbance under sunlight unless formulated with stabilisers such as octocrylene [1][2][3].

In 2019 and 2020, randomised trials sponsored by the US Food and Drug Administration (FDA) found that avobenzone and other sunscreen ingredients enter the bloodstream after topical use at concentrations above the 0.5 ng/mL threshold the agency had set for further safety study [4][5]. The authors and regulators stated that this finding does not by itself show that the ingredients are unsafe.

paras: Avobenzone is added to sunscreens, daytime moisturisers and makeup to absorb UVA radiation, which is associated with photoageing and skin cancer. FDA-listed products such as SPF 15 facial moisturisers combine it with homosalate, octisalate and octocrylene and carry label claims of helping prevent sunburn and decreasing the risk of skin cancer and early skin ageing when used with other sun protection measures [6]. Within looksmaxxing and skincare communities, sunscreen use is commonly discussed as an anti-ageing measure.

Avobenzone is a dibenzoylmethane derivative that exists mostly in the enol form and is insoluble in water [2]. Under sunlight its absorbance falls substantially; data cited by Wikipedia show a 36% drop after an hour of sun exposure [2]. Formulators therefore pair it with photostabilisers such as octocrylene, and studies of filter combinations have compared how well different mixtures retain their protection [3]. Mineral filters such as zinc oxide and titanium dioxide can accelerate its breakdown unless particles are coated [2].

A 2019 randomised trial under maximal-use conditions and a 2020 trial of six active ingredients, including avobenzone, oxybenzone, octocrylene, homosalate, octisalate and octinoxate, measured blood levels after sunscreen application and found systemic absorption [4][5]. A phase 1 registration of the same programme enrolled 72 participants [7]. These studies measured absorption, not clinical harm.

In 2021 the FDA said avobenzone was not currently classed as generally recognised as safe and effective, citing the need for more safety data, and Palau banned it in 2020 over reef concerns [2]. A 2017 laboratory study reported that chlorinated water and UV light can break avobenzone into other compounds [2]. UV filters in general have been detected in lake water and wastewater [8][9].

Human studies have mostly examined avobenzone as one ingredient among several in finished sunscreens. The 2019 and 2020 JAMA trials measured plasma concentrations and found systemic absorption [4][5]. A study of UVA exposure and singlet oxygen in skin (NCT05865431) enrolled 17 people [10], and a 2009 sunscreen SPF study in 10 participants is registered [11]. These do not test avobenzone alone for appearance outcomes.

timeline.event: JAMA maximal-use trial reports systemic absorption of sunscreen ingredients [5].
Second JAMA trial extends findings to six ingredients; Palau ban takes effect [4][2].
FDA states it does not consider avobenzone generally recognised as safe and effective pending more data [2].

card.summary: The main organic UVA filter in US sunscreens: widely used for photoageing protection, unstable in sunlight without stabilisers, absorbed into the bloodstream.
card.note: FDA says more safety data are needed; it is photounstable.

quick.overview:
Avobenzone is a chemical sunscreen filter that absorbs UVA light, the part of sunlight linked to photoageing. It is found in many sunscreens and SPF moisturisers.

It breaks down in sunlight unless paired with stabilisers like octocrylene. FDA-sponsored trials found it is absorbed into the blood after application.
quick.mechanism: Its conjugated structure absorbs UVA photons and releases the energy as heat, reducing UV reaching skin cells [1].
quick.risks: Regulators have asked for more safety data on systemic absorption; the studies measured blood levels, not harm. Allergy and environmental concerns have been reported, and Palau banned it in 2020 [2]. It is OTC; limits are 3% in the US and 5% in the EU.
